rationale: Although the study empirically evaluates progress toward universal drinking water access across developing countries (meeting C1, C3, and C4), its exposure of interest is macro-level water sector spending and the aggregate volume of international development aid rather than a legal, administrative, regulatory, tariff/subsidy rule, tenure, enforcement, or institutional mechanism governing service access (failing Criterion 2; E03 wrong exposure).
plain_vs_narrow_note: Both narrow and plain readings of Criterion 2 result in exclusion (E03) because the study examines aggregate sector spending and macro-level international aid volumes rather than any legal, administrative, regulatory, institutional, or governance mechanism governing household or community water access.

evidence_quotes.quote: Financing and the role of aid within the water sector are poorly understood.
Longitudinal analysis shows no detectable effect of volume of aid on progress.
As the world approaches universal access to improved water, aid must increasingly focus on sustaining progress and assisting countries that still have sizable unserved populations.
